units.text: Suppose we have before us the entire history of a universe: every event, without mistakes or gaps. Would anything remain to learn about its laws? The question separates several philosophies that can accept the same experiments and interpret differently what those experiments tell us exists.

The Humean tradition begins with the distribution of facts. In the best-system approach associated with David Lewis, laws are not additional commands issued to events. They belong to the system achieving a privileged balance among simplicity, informative power and, for probabilistic theories, fit with the facts. Not every convenient summary becomes a law (Carroll, 2020) .

The advantage is ontological economy. We do not introduce an invisible administrator of necessity alongside events and properties. The difficulty is that simplicity sometimes seems vocabulary-dependent: what is complicated in one notation may be short in another. Another concern arises: if laws depend on the entirety of history, in what sense do they explain the very history they summarize? A defender of this position may reply that an explanation need not be a separate cause of the facts.

Armstrong proposes another direction. Laws are relations among general properties, called universals, not merely coincidences among particular cases. The relationship among universals would support the pattern’s necessitating character. This conception tries to distinguish a genuine regularity from a merely repeated accident within the world’s own structure (Armstrong, 1983) .

The price is a new question: what makes the relation among universals compel particular instances? If we answer only ‘it is a relation of necessity’, have we offered an explanation or named the problem? The objection is not fatal by definition; every theory reaches elements it no longer explains through others. But where explanation stops must be made visible.

A third family emphasizes powers and dispositions. An object would not be a mere bearer of labels awaiting external commands; its properties would include ways of reacting. A glass’s fragility refers to what would happen in certain circumstances even if the glass is never broken. Laws might express these powers. Within the broader debate, positions on dispositions are not identical and do not all imply the existence of separate fundamental laws (Carroll, 2020) .

This picture has an intuitive merit: it places order within things. It also has a difficulty: if we identify a property only by what it produces and explain the production through the property, we risk circularity. To avoid mere wordplay, we must show independent relationships among manifestations, conditions and structures.

Maudlin defends treating fundamental laws as irreducible elements of ontology. Not every fundamental notion in physics must be reconstructible from an inventory of lawless facts. Some things may be primary in explanation. His position directly challenges the Humean reduction project (Maudlin, 2007) .

The answer is intellectually respectable but unsatisfying to anyone always asking ‘why?’ Laws would be what explains, not what still needs explanation. Yet the opponent does not automatically escape a stopping point: they may leave the total distribution of facts unexplained. The dispute is partly about where we accept a basic fact.

Nancy Cartwright challenges the assumption that the success of laws in controlled arrangements automatically authorizes a uniform picture of the entire world. The metaphor of the ‘dappled’ world foregrounds capacities, local conditions and mechanisms producing regularities. The lesson for science is to investigate conditions for transporting a result, not assume a formula travels without baggage. This is a philosophical thesis about the power and limits of laws, not an experimental verdict that any unification is impossible (Cartwright, 1999) .

Finally, we can be cautious about all these ontologies. Constructive empiricism associated with Bas van Fraassen demands empirical adequacy without requiring belief in the complete truth of the unobservable description. Structural realism, in different forms, places special trust in relationships or structures preserved by theories even when the picture of objects changes. They are not the same program: one limits commitment; the other selects it (Chakravartty, 2017) .

This book’s working position is a critical realism of constraints. Some relationships resist us and permit stable interventions. This is a reason not to treat the world as arbitrary fiction. But from a constraint’s robustness we do not automatically deduce that we have discovered a legislator, an ultimate necessity or the only possible description. We can have excellent reasons to use a law and insufficient reasons to declare its metaphysics settled.
